name: ffe
desc: Parse flat file structures and print them in different formats
why: Parses flat file structures like COBOL-era records and prints them; an old-school file format explorer that is a close call.

brief.what_it_is: ffe (Flat File Extractor) is a command-line tool for parsing flat file structures, both text and fixed-length binary, and printing the results in other formats. It reads standard input and writes standard output by default. Input structure and output format are both user-configurable rather than predefined, and it tries to guess the input format so the user does not have to supply it. Output options named on the homepage include fixed length, separated, tokenized, XML, SQL, and raw.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as a way to extract fields or records from flat files, convert between formats such as CSV and fixed length, verify a flat file structure, and act as a testing tool for flat file development.
brief.how_it_works: Input file structure and output definitions are kept separate, so one output format can be applied to several input files. One input file can hold several record types (lines or binary blocks). The homepage does not describe the internal parsing mechanism beyond this.
brief.install_notes: The homepage says ffe is built with GNU autotools, so it should build on many UNIX-like systems. Source and a Windows executable are on SourceForge, and Debian packages and a FreeBSD port are listed. The homepage does not describe any runtime, account, or configuration requirements.
brief.standout: It is an old-school, configurable parser for fixed-length COBOL-style and binary records, with a field-level output format selector, lookup tables, and a simple anonymization option (-A). Most of the tools you would compare it to handle delimited text rather than fixed-length binary blocks.
brief.status: quiet. The most recent item in the News section is version 0.3.9 dated 2018-11-04, and the homepage shows no later release or commit. I did not check SourceForge or the Debian/FreeBSD packages, so the status is inferred from the homepage only.
brief.caveats: The homepage says it was developed in a GNU/Linux environment, and the Windows executable is only mentioned under Download. It is GPL v2 or later. The homepage does not say how many distributions currently package it. I did not read the full manual, so feature completeness is unverified.
